extracted.intended_audience: legal scholars, economists, and policymakers concerned with patent policy
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the functions and institutional features of the patent system (especially the U.S. system) with implications for patent policy and welfare; introduces the 'prospect theory' of patents and contrasts it with the conventional 'reward theory.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Prospect function of the patent system
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent system performs a 'prospect' function: by awarding exclusive and publicly recorded ownership of a prospect shortly after its discovery, it tends to assure efficient allocation of resources among prospects, place management of each prospect in the entity best equipped to manage it, and cause information found by one entity to be communicated to others at an efficient rate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This conception treats technological innovation as searches over prospects with varying costs and returns and views patents as analogous to mineral claims that organize investment and development of opportunities. Use this criterion to evaluate whether patent rules (scope, timing, recording, transferability) promote efficient allocation and management of innovation resources.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reward theory (patent as inventor's capture of returns)
rubrics_metrics.description: The conventional 'reward theory' views the patent as a reward enabling an inventor to capture returns from his investment in the invention, tending to make private investment closer to the value of its social product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize this as the traditional justificatory standard against which other patent features are judged; consider both the incentive benefits and the welfare loss from exclusive control when demand is downward-sloping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of patent claims often exceeds the inventor's concrete contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent claims are 'an abstraction and generalization of an indefinitely large number of concrete, physical objects' and thus reach beyond what the reward theory would require; broad claims can cover later-developed superior embodiments or unforeseen uses (examples: fat separation, Selden automobile combination, diode patent covering triode, new therapeutic uses for a chemical).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate claim scope not only by the inventor's actual reduced embodiment but by the abstract claim language; anticipate that broad claims may preempt later improvements or alternative practical implementations and consider how such scope supports the prospect function (early reservation of an opportunity) while raising antipatent concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority and early-filing rules force early patent applications
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules awarding priority to the first to file (or first inventor in U.S. practice) create strong incentives to file as soon as a working version is found; senior/junior status and demanding standards of proof for prior inventorship make early filing practically decisive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how priority rules influence timing of applications and whether they cause claim-staking early in development (supporting prospect reservation) even when commercial value is uncertain. Note the 'near miss' risk where second discoverers lose rights regardless of relative investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-bar and public disclosure rules pressure timely filing
rubrics_metrics.description: Time-bar rules (e.g., invalidity if application is filed more than one year after commercial use or after publication describing the invention) make late filing risky and thus force early patenting; commercial use or publication by others can trigger the bar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider how statutory bars (such as 35 U.S.C. §102(b) described) limit strategic delays and encourage prompt patent applications even in the absence of commercial readiness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Low threshold for patentable disclosure (constructive reduction to practice)
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent application need only disclose an invention that 'works' (a constructive reduction to practice) and does not need to show that the invention is fully developed or commercially valuable (e.g., a battery must produce current; a copying process must make copies in some sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating whether patents are being used to reserve prospects, note that the legal standard allows modest or imperfect embodiments to secure patent rights, thus enabling early claim-staking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be delimited to the inventor's invention; overbroad claims are invalid
rubrics_metrics.description: The applicant must limit his claims to his invention in the claims portion of the patent document; if claims exceed the invention they are invalid (analogous to the mineral-claim boundary rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess claim drafting and scope carefully: the patent system requires specific delimitation in claims and boundary description, and these legal limits are a central evaluative criterion for validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analogous institutional features between patents and mineral claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The patent system parallels the American mineral-claim system in many respects: (1) neither requires demonstration of commercial significance to stake a claim; (2) priority is awarded to the first to discover/stake/file; (3) claims/boundaries must be specified; (4) there are obligations/mechanisms to return unpromising claims to the public (mining work vs. patent term/maintenance); (5) interests can be transferred before/after rights are established.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this analogy to evaluate institutional design choices (staking/filing requirements, claim scope, transferability, maintenance obligations) and how they affect incentives to search and develop technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited patent term and maintenance requirements serve to weed out unpromising claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The mineral system's annual work requirement is paralleled in the patent system by a limited patent term (and in some systems by maintenance payments), which returns unpromising prospects to the public domain when the owner chooses not to continue investment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider patent term and maintenance regimes as instruments to ensure that holders continue to invest in valuable prospects; evaluate whether these mechanisms effectively cause abandonment of low-value claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents are often issued long before commercial exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: Many technologically important patents have been issued long before commercial exploitation became possible; case studies show first patentable inventions frequently precede first significant commercial products by years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When analysing the timing and effects of patents, account for the frequent gap between patenting and commercial viability; this is evidence of the prospect-reservation role of patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent ownership facilitates coordination, reduces duplication, and enables information exchange
rubrics_metrics.description: Exclusive ownership (a patent 'prospect') improves the efficiency of managing investment in innovation by enabling the owner to coordinate searches for technological and market enhancements, avoid duplicative investments, and exchange information among searchers—advantages particularly important because technological investigation can be done in secrecy and leave no visible trace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate patent regimes by their capacity to enable coordination among investors and developers; pay attention to how secrecy and lack of signaling in R&D amplify the potential benefits of exclusive rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of patent property rights depends on demand conditions and must be assessed case-by-case
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether the gains from unified control (efficiency of investment and realization of prospects) exceed the welfare losses from monopoly pricing depends on the demand conditions faced by individual patents; altering rights on a case-by-case basis would be administratively costly and create uncertainty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy conclusions should consider heterogeneity across technologies and markets; blanket assertions about patents increasing or reducing output are inadequate—analysis should examine specific demand and competitive circumstances.
